findings.title: Recovery codes validated against user storage are never consumed and remain reusable
findings.body: When the recovery-codes credential lives in local storage, the code that was just used is consumed as a side effect of validation (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid removes the used code and persists the credential). When the credential lives in user storage (the new path added by this PR), validation is delegated to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid, and nothing afterwards marks the code as used: there is no updateCredential/disableCredentialType callback with the remaining codes. The test provider added in this PR demonstrates the gap — BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid only checks membership in the stored raw-code list and never removes the used entry, so the same recovery code can be presented again on every subsequent login. This silently weakens the one-time-use security property of recovery codes for exactly the scenario this PR enables, and the new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) never asserts that a used code is invalidated. Either Keycloak should push the remaining codes back via updateCredential after a successful user-storage validation, or the limitation should be explicitly handled/documented.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById cannot remove a user-storage (federated) recovery-codes credential
findings.body: After this change the credential looked up via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential may come from user storage (getFederatedCredentialsStream). If such a provider tracks used codes itself and returns a credential whose allCodesUsed() is true, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...) only removes credentials from the local store and silently does nothing for federated credentials — additionally, credential models built by a storage provider (as the test provider does with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues) may carry a null or synthetic id, so the removal has no valid target. The exhausted credential then remains in user storage, isConfiguredFor keeps returning true, and the user continues to be challenged with recovery codes that can never succeed. Removal for federated credentials would need to go through the storage provider (e.g. updateCredential/disableCredentialType) instead of removeStoredCredentialById.
